title: From Chai Pani to Cal-India Collective: Indian Cuisine Earns Its Biggest-Ever Haul at the 2026 James Beard Awards
excerpt: With multiple Indian-origin chefs and restaurateurs nominated across national categories, this year's ceremony on June 15 could mark a turning point for South Asian food in America.
body:
When the James Beard Foundation released its 2026 finalist list this spring, Indian food occupied more lines than it ever has in the awards' 36-year history. Not one chef in one city, but a constellation of restaurateurs, cookbook authors, and culinary entrepreneurs spanning the country — from Asheville, North Carolina, to Palo Alto, California, to the heart of Chicago. On June 15, when winners are announced at the Lyric Opera of Chicago, Indian cuisine could walk away with the kind of recognition that historically eluded it.

## The Outstanding Restaurateur Race

The most significant nominations may be in the Outstanding Restaurateur category, which honours not a single dish or dining room but the sustained vision of building community through restaurants. Two of the five finalists this year are Indian-origin.

**Srijith Gopinathan and Ayesha Thapar** lead Cal-India Collective, the hospitality group behind Ettan, Copra, Eylan, and Little Blue Door across Palo Alto, San Francisco, Menlo Park, and Los Altos. Gopinathan, who previously earned two Michelin stars at Campton Place, has built a portfolio that spans South Indian fine dining, Goan seafood, and modern Indian cocktail bars — a rare example of an Indian restaurateur successfully scaling a multi-concept group in America's most competitive dining market.

**Meherwan and Molly Irani** of the Chai Pani Restaurant Group bring a very different story. Chai Pani started as a single street-food counter in Asheville in 2009, serving bhel puri, kati rolls, and chaat to a city better known for craft beer and Appalachian cooking. Sixteen years later, it has become an institution — with the flagship and its counter-service sibling Botiwalla now in multiple locations, including Washington, D.C. The Iranis' nomination validates the idea that Indian food can succeed not just in coastal metros with large diaspora populations, but in the American heartland.

## Chefs Pushing Boundaries

In the Best Chef categories, Indian-origin chefs appeared across multiple regions. **Sujan Sarkar** of Indienne in Chicago was named a semifinalist in the Great Lakes category for his avant-garde Indian tasting menus that draw from classical French technique and Bengali culinary tradition. Sarkar's work represents the cutting edge of what Indian fine dining can be in America — dishes that are unmistakably Indian in flavour but unconstrained by format.

**Nur-E Gulshan Rahman** of Korai Kitchen in Jersey City earned a semifinalist nod in the Mid-Atlantic, representing the Bangladeshi-Indian culinary continuum that is reshaping the food scene in the greater New York area. Meanwhile, in New York itself, Time Out Market's Union Square food hall recently welcomed **Kebabwala** from Unapologetic Foods — the same group behind Michelin-starred Semma — bringing their South Indian sensibility to a high-traffic counter-service format alongside concepts from Kwame Onwuachi and other celebrated chefs.

## Books and Beyond the Kitchen

The Indian presence extends beyond the kitchen to the bookshelf. **Sapna Punjabi's** *Dal Chawal*, a collection of 85 vegetarian lentil-and-rice recipes rooted in Ayurvedic tradition, is a finalist in the Vegetable-Focused Cooking category. And *MUMBAI: A Journey Through Its Kitchens, Streets, and Stories* by **Rushina Munshaw Ghildiyal** is nominated in the Visuals category — a lavish exploration of the city's culinary geography that brings Bombay's street-food culture to the coffee-table format.

Together, these nominations paint a picture of Indian food that is no longer auditioning for mainstream acceptance but demanding recognition on its own terms.

## What Changed

The shift did not happen overnight. Chef Vijay Kumar's 2025 win as Best Chef in New York State — for Semma, the South Indian restaurant that introduced goat brain masala and Chettinad cooking to Greenwich Village — cracked open a door. Kumar's emotional acceptance speech, in which he said he never imagined "a dark-skinned boy from Tamil Nadu" could stand in such a room, became a defining moment for Indian food in America.

But the 2026 class is notable for its breadth. It is not one chef or one cuisine but many: Tamil and Bengali, Goan and street-food, clinical dietetics and photographic storytelling. The James Beard Foundation's expanded semifinalist pool, which now spans hundreds of nominees, has helped surface Indian talent that was previously invisible to the awards' New York–centric radar.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the nearly five million Indian Americans watching from home — many of whom grew up being told their food was "too smelly" or "too spicy" for school lunchboxes — the 2026 James Beard class carries an emotional charge that the foundation's judges may not fully grasp. It is validation, yes, but also visibility. Every nomination tells a young Indian-American cook or aspiring restaurateur that the flavours they grew up with are worthy of the country's highest culinary honour.

The ceremony takes place on June 15 at the Lyric Opera of Chicago. Whether Indian food walks away with hardware or not, the nomination slate alone has already rewritten the story.

*Sources: James Beard Foundation, Restaurant Business Online, Bhasha Times, Curly Tales, The Indian Eye*
